## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

# Todo

This file contains near term tasks with a short description
and reference links to more details.

Intro paragraphs in `## Todo` and `## Bugs` should begin every
line with 1 leading space so they don't match the `^\d+\. `
pattern that locates numbered entries; 2 or 3 spaces also work.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text **moves** here
(never copied; one home per text). The picked-up task is a
`###` heading; a multi-cycle program adds one level, where the
program is the `###` and its current stage a `####` (headings
give the current work durable anchors, which numbered Todo
entries can't). The problem overview is followed by the
"plan", a bulleted list of the development "ladder". Each
rung is prepended with its commit reference, a literal
`[[N]]` placeholder until the commit is pushed, then
backfilled to a real file-local `[[n]]` ref (same pattern as
the chores As-built rungs):
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

### Refactor: typed jj facade -> jj-lib in-process; end subprocess spawning

Version-control operations were ~30 hand-rolled `run("jj", ...)`
spawns plus every mutation, with per-module private wrappers
and raw-git vestiges in init: stderr parsing instead of typed
errors, and jj's single-attempt index-lock acquisition (the
push `bookmark-set` lock race in [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md))
can't be retried where it fails. A multi-ladder program; the
staged plan, design detail, and the eight absorbed former
Todos live in
[refactor-20260716.md](notes/refactor-20260716.md).

Program ladder in **straight trunk order**, one bullet per
commit that lands on the branch, so reading it top to bottom
is reading `git log --first-parent`. `refactor:` entries are
the program's rungs, one per cycle (adjacent stages
consolidated 2026-07-24; titles are the anticipated close-out
titles; unshipped versions are provisional, since jj-lib may
split into two cycles). `docs:` entries are interludes that
sit between cycles and belong to no rung. Every shipped ref
points at a close-out commit on `refactor-vc-x1`, treated as
permanent: the branch is long-lived and lands on main
merge-only, never rebased.

The order is load-bearing: a
trapezoid's `<base>` is the parent of its own first rung, not
the previous close-out, so 0.78.0 bases on 0.77.4. Taking the
close-out instead swallows the interludes into the merge's
ladder side, which already bit at 0.76.0, whose base was the
0.75.1 interlude. See
[the recipe](notes/cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe).

1	# Code conventions
2	
3	Conventions for source code. Read this before writing code. The Rust-specific sections apply
4	wherever the medium is a Rust crate (see [custom.md](../custom.md) for the project's medium).
5	
6	Universal file, pinned to vc-x1-work-repo-template; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
7	[custom.md](../custom.md).
8	
9	## Line width
10	
11	Source lines, including doc comments and inline comments, wrap at <=100 cols (rustfmt's
12	default `max_width`; the per-commit flow's `cargo fmt` enforces it for code, and the same limit
13	applies to the comment text it doesn't reflow).
14	
15	## Doc comments on every file, function, and method
16	
17	Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every function and method must have
18	a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief: one sentence of purpose is often enough; the discipline
19	is that the comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
20	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).
21	
22	This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to
23	inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected; inline
24	explanatory comments inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
25	non-obvious WHY.
26	
27	**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows
28	by default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
29	any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered
30	help.
31	
32	## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)
33	
34	The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
35	`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
36	patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a
37	lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
38	in scope:
39	
40	- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
41	- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a
42	  silently substituted value that can hide a wrong result.
43	
44	When one is used, three obligations attach:
45	
46	- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
47	  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
48	    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
49	  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
50	    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
51	  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are
52	    not used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
53	- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and
54	  appropriate uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
55	- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site, because Rust projects
56	  enable the project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`:
57	
58	  ```toml
59	  [lints.clippy]
60	  unwrap_used = "warn"
61	  expect_used = "warn"
62	  ```
63	
64	  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff; clippy (in the per-commit flow)
65	  catches any that slip through. The `_or*` siblings have no clippy lint; they are covered by

# Code conventions

Conventions for source code. Read this before writing code. The Rust-specific sections apply
wherever the medium is a Rust crate (see [custom.md](../custom.md) for the project's medium).

Universal file, pinned to vc-x1-work-repo-template; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
[custom.md](../custom.md).

## Line width

Source lines, including doc comments and inline comments, wrap at <=100 cols (rustfmt's
default `max_width`; the per-commit flow's `cargo fmt` enforces it for code, and the same limit
applies to the comment text it doesn't reflow).

## Doc comments on every file, function, and method

Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every function and method must have
a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief: one sentence of purpose is often enough; the discipline
is that the comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).

This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to
inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected; inline
explanatory comments inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
non-obvious WHY.

**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows
by default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered
help.

## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a
lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
in scope:

- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a
  silently substituted value that can hide a wrong result.

When one is used, three obligations attach:

- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are
    not used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and
  appropriate uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site, because Rust projects
  enable the project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`:

  ```toml
  [lints.clippy]
  unwrap_used = "warn"
  expect_used = "warn"
  ```

  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff; clippy (in the per-commit flow)
  catches any that slip through. The `_or*` siblings have no clippy lint; they are covered by
  the comment convention and the conversational alert. (The vc-x1-work-repo-template's
  `CargoRust.toml` seeds a base `Cargo.toml` with this section already in place.)

```rust
let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious

match matches.len() {
    1 => {
        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
    }
    // ...
}
```

Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt, since panicking on setup failure is the correct test
behavior.

1	//! Typed facade over `jj` subprocess queries.
2	//!
3	//! Every read-only `jj log -T <template>` / `jj bookmark list`
4	//! spawn goes through this module — primitives plus typed
5	//! helpers — so call sites stop hand-rolling argument lists (the
6	//! DRY-facade stage of `notes/refactor-20260716.md`):
7	//!
8	//! - `log` — the raw primitive; the helpers below cover the
9	//!   common templates.
10	//! - `matches` / `rev_exists` — does a revset match / does a
11	//!   revision resolve.
12	//! - `chid_of` / `cid_of` / `cid_short_of` — change / commit ids.
13	//! - `desc_of` / `is_empty` — description and emptiness.
14	//!
15	//! Mutations still spawn `jj` at their call sites; the jj-lib
16	//! migration stage moves both in-process.
17	
18	use std::path::Path;
19	
20	use crate::common::run;
21	
22	/// Crate-standard boxed-error result, aliased locally for brevity.
23	type Result<T> = std::result::Result<T, Box<dyn std::error::Error>>;
24	
25	/// Run `jj log -r <rev> --no-graph -T <template> -R <repo>` and
26	/// return its stdout (`run` trims surrounding whitespace).
27	pub fn log(repo: &Path, rev: &str, template: &str) -> Result<String> {
28	    run(
29	        "jj",
30	        &[
31	            "log",
32	            "-r",
33	            rev,
34	            "--no-graph",
35	            "-T",
36	            template,
37	            "-R",
38	            &repo.to_string_lossy(),
39	        ],
40	        Path::new("."),
41	    )
42	}
43	
44	/// True when `revset` matches at least one commit in `repo`.
45	///
46	/// A valid-but-empty revset (e.g. `conflicts()` on a clean repo)
47	/// is `Ok(false)`; an unresolvable revision is an `Err` — use
48	/// `rev_exists` to fold that case to `false`.
49	pub fn matches(repo: &Path, revset: &str) -> Result<bool> {
50	    Ok(!log(repo, revset, "\"x\"")?.is_empty())
51	}
52	
53	/// True when `rev` resolves in `repo`.
54	///
55	/// Maps jj's unresolvable-revision errors (`doesn't exist`,
56	/// `No such revision`) to `Ok(false)`; other failures (bad repo
57	/// path, spawn error) stay `Err`.
58	pub fn rev_exists(repo: &Path, rev: &str) -> Result<bool> {
59	    match matches(repo, rev) {
60	        Ok(found) => Ok(found),
61	        Err(e) => {
62	            let msg = e.to_string();
63	            if msg.contains("doesn't exist") || msg.contains("No such revision") {
64	                Ok(false)
65	            } else {
66	                Err(e)
67	            }
68	        }
69	    }
70	}
71	
72	/// The 12-character change id of `rev`.
73	pub fn chid_of(repo: &Path, rev: &str) -> Result<String> {
74	    log(repo, rev, "change_id.short(12)")
75	}
76	
77	/// The full commit id of `rev`.
78	pub fn cid_of(repo: &Path, rev: &str) -> Result<String> {
79	    log(repo, rev, "commit_id")
80	}
81	
82	/// The 12-character commit id of `rev`.
83	pub fn cid_short_of(repo: &Path, rev: &str) -> Result<String> {
84	    log(repo, rev, "commit_id.short(12)")
85	}
86	
87	/// The full description (title + body) of `rev`.
88	pub fn desc_of(repo: &Path, rev: &str) -> Result<String> {
89	    log(repo, rev, "description")
90	}
91	
92	/// True when `rev` is empty (no file changes relative to its
93	/// parent). Strict: anything but `true` / `false` from the
94	/// template is an error.
95	pub fn is_empty(repo: &Path, rev: &str) -> Result<bool> {
96	    let out = log(repo, rev, "empty")?;
97	    match out.as_str() {
98	        "true" => Ok(true),
99	        "false" => Ok(false),
100	        other => Err(format!("jj::is_empty: unexpected template output {other:?}").into()),
101	    }
102	}
103	
104	/// Run `jj bookmark list <bookmark> -R <repo>` and return its
105	/// stdout — empty when the local bookmark doesn't exist.
106	pub fn bookmark_list(repo: &Path, bookmark: &str) -> Result<String> {
107	    run(
108	        "jj",
109	        &["bookmark", "list", bookmark, "-R", &repo.to_string_lossy()],
110	        Path::new("."),
111	    )
112	}
113	
114	/// Like `bookmark_list` but with `-a`: includes remote refs —
115	/// tracked ones indented (`  @origin: …`), non-tracking at
116	/// column 0 (`<bookmark>@<remote>: …`). The input for
117	/// `common::find_tracked_remote` /
118	/// `common::find_non_tracking_remote`.
119	pub fn bookmark_list_all(repo: &Path, bookmark: &str) -> Result<String> {
120	    run(
121	        "jj",
122	        &[
123	            "bookmark",
124	            "list",
125	            "-a",
126	            bookmark,
127	            "-R",
128	            &repo.to_string_lossy(),
129	        ],
130	        Path::new("."),
131	    )
132	}

`Commits: [[3]]`, or `Commits: [[3]],[[5]]` for several. (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the
`[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]` resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and
CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The `# References` definition puts the **commit
URL** as the destination, with the **full 40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
  say) gets the canonical identifier.

**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every section opens with an
**empty `Commits:`**, and each push backfills the `Commits:` of the commits the previous push
made permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands. The commit itself is
the record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
[Commits backfill](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).

1	# Prose and durable text
2	
3	How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
4	commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
5	comments, chores sections).
6	
7	Universal file, pinned to vc-x1-work-repo-template; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
8	[custom.md](../custom.md).
9	
10	## Prose form
11	
12	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why*
13	or the high-level *what*, then a `-` bullet list for the details. Wrap lines at <=100 cols,
14	commit titles and bodies at <=72 (bullet continuations indent two spaces); existing text
15	re-wraps when touched, no mass sweeps. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they hide the structure
16	that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their relationship is
17	the same failure at sentence scale; see [Semicolons inside bullets](#semicolons-inside-bullets)
18	and [Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
19	
20	Surfaces that use this shape:
21	
22	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files; see
23	  [Doc comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
24	- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The <=72-col title is the
25	  commit-specific add-on; see [Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
26	- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`; see
27	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
28	- Todo and Done entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure
29	  one-liners are still fine.
30	
31	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
32	
33	- **Commit bodies**: bullets are file-by-file, one bullet per file changed, file plus a
34	  one-line gist (e.g. `README.md: new Overview intro`), detail as sub-bullets in short sentence
35	  fragments (full sentences are discouraged). Source of truth for the mechanical edit list.
36	- **Chores / todo / done**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what
37	  landed and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit
38	  list; see
39	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
40	- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).
41	
42	### Problem + plan shape
43	
44	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores section intros, and `## Todo` entries use a sharper form
45	of the same shape:
46	
47	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences; don't pad with intent, don't restate
48	  the plan.
49	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when): formality differs by surface:
50	  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per commit; see
51	    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
52	    per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
53	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering; formalized only when the entry is
54	    picked up into a cycle.
55	
56	### Semicolons inside bullets
57	
58	A bullet that joins multiple clauses with semicolons (`A; B; C`) is a list hiding inside
59	running prose: break the clauses into sub-bullets so the structure shows. Semicolons in running
60	prose (intro paragraphs, sentence-joins) are fine. Not absolute: very short clauses or tight
61	pairs can stay joined inside a bullet when breaking would be more noise than signal.
62	
63	### Typeable punctuation only
64	
65	Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. Banned: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`.
66	None can be entered without a compose key or a paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em
67	dash next to option syntax reads as another flag. Unlike the semicolon rule above this one is
68	absolute: they cost nothing to write and are paid on every read, so a soft rule accumulates
69	them.
70	
71	`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em
72	dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:
73	
74	- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
75	  sub-bullets.
76	- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a
77	  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
78	- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just
79	  go.
80	
81	Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive,
82	so `## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
83	[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same
84	commit.
85	
86	Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and
87	everything under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is
88	the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
89	prose. It applies going forward; existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
90	by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.
91	A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
92	`` `.expect(...)` ``.
93	
94	Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
95	commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits
96	in a code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching
97	`git log --grep` and breaks the verbatim identity that
98	[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) requires between
99	a commit title, its chores header, and its `## Done` entry.
100	
101	### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)
102	
103	A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description share a *title* shape, a
104	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`,
105	an optional `(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail.
106	They differ in the title's prefix / marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies are
107	file-by-file, ladder / chores conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface" above). The
108	shared template:
109	
110	```
111	<optional - X.Y.Z[-N]> <title>   # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
112	<optional prose intro>
113	  - <optional item>
114	    <optional prose intro>
115	      - <optional sub-item>
116	      ...
117	```
118	
119	The three surfaces apply it as:
120	
121	- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the title is prefixed with the version
122	  (`X.Y.Z-N <title>`) and carries a `(current)` / `(done)` marker. The bare three-element
123	  `X.Y.Z` (no `-N`) is the close-out step. Detail is bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
124	- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no version prefix, since the `##` header
125	  *is* the bare title, with a `Commits: [[ref]]` line first under it (empty until backfilled;
126	  see [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
127	- **Commit description**: no version prefix, and the title is the <=72-col first line; the body
128	  is the prose (file-by-file for the work repo, per
129	  [Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow)).
130	
131	The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a step's ladder entry, its
132	chores `##` header, and its commit title line up verbatim; pick the commit title first and
133	reuse it.
134	
135	That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct
136	descriptive title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
137	section header carries the anticipated *close-out* title. To keep a cycle's commits collectable
138	with one `git log --grep`, give the step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).
139	
140	## Speculation marker
141	
142	Durable text the bot writes (instruction files, `notes/`, commit bodies, chores sections)
143	should stick to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism,
144	hypothesis, or causal claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
145	reader can tell the measured from the inferred.
146	
147	**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader (or the bot on a later
148	session) can pick it up as a known fact when it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction
149	worth keeping visible in the written record.
150	
151	**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with
152	"We think ..." (or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism
153	("X wins because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a
154	prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data
155	on hand.
156	
157	## Plain synopsis after technical explanations
158	
159	When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation (measurement theory, statistics,
160	hardware behavior), end it with a short plain-language synopsis, no jargon and no symbols, so
161	the reader can check their understanding against the technical version.
162	
163	**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread; the plain form catches
164	misunderstandings early, when they are cheap.
165	
166	**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (a notes entry should already lead with
167	the why). Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no
168	synopsis.

and [Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).

Surfaces that use this shape:

- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files; see
  [Doc comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The <=72-col title is the
  commit-specific add-on; see [Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`; see
  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- Todo and Done entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure
  one-liners are still fine.

Bullet *content* differs by surface:

- **Commit bodies**: bullets are file-by-file, one bullet per file changed, file plus a
  one-line gist (e.g. `README.md: new Overview intro`), detail as sub-bullets in short sentence
  fragments (full sentences are discouraged). Source of truth for the mechanical edit list.
- **Chores / todo / done**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what
  landed and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit
  list; see
  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).

### Problem + plan shape

`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores section intros, and `## Todo` entries use a sharper form
of the same shape:

- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences; don't pad with intent, don't restate
  the plan.
- **Plan bullets** (the what/when): formality differs by surface:
  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per commit; see
    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
    per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering; formalized only when the entry is
    picked up into a cycle.

### Semicolons inside bullets

A bullet that joins multiple clauses with semicolons (`A; B; C`) is a list hiding inside
running prose: break the clauses into sub-bullets so the structure shows. Semicolons in running
prose (intro paragraphs, sentence-joins) are fine. Not absolute: very short clauses or tight
pairs can stay joined inside a bullet when breaking would be more noise than signal.

### Typeable punctuation only

Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. Banned: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`.
None can be entered without a compose key or a paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em
dash next to option syntax reads as another flag. Unlike the semicolon rule above this one is
absolute: they cost nothing to write and are paid on every read, so a soft rule accumulates
them.

`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em
dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
  sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a
  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just
  go.

Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive,
so `## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same
commit.

Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and
everything under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is
the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
prose. It applies going forward; existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.
A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
`` `.expect(...)` ``.

Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits
in a code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching
`git log --grep` and breaks the verbatim identity that
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) requires between
a commit title, its chores header, and its `## Done` entry.

### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)

A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description share a *title* shape, a
[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`,
an optional `(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail.
They differ in the title's prefix / marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies are
file-by-file, ladder / chores conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface" above). The
shared template:

```
<optional - X.Y.Z[-N]> <title>   # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
<optional prose intro>
  - <optional item>
    <optional prose intro>
      - <optional sub-item>
      ...
```

The three surfaces apply it as:

- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the title is prefixed with the version
  (`X.Y.Z-N <title>`) and carries a `(current)` / `(done)` marker. The bare three-element
  `X.Y.Z` (no `-N`) is the close-out step. Detail is bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no version prefix, since the `##` header
  *is* the bare title, with a `Commits: [[ref]]` line first under it (empty until backfilled;
  see [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
- **Commit description**: no version prefix, and the title is the <=72-col first line; the body
  is the prose (file-by-file for the work repo, per
  [Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow)).

The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a step's ladder entry, its
chores `##` header, and its commit title line up verbatim; pick the commit title first and
reuse it.

That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct
descriptive title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
section header carries the anticipated *close-out* title. To keep a cycle's commits collectable
with one `git log --grep`, give the step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).

## Speculation marker

Durable text the bot writes (instruction files, `notes/`, commit bodies, chores sections)
should stick to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism,
hypothesis, or causal claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
reader can tell the measured from the inferred.

**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader (or the bot on a later
session) can pick it up as a known fact when it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction
worth keeping visible in the written record.

**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with
"We think ..." (or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism
("X wins because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a
prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data
on hand.

## Plain synopsis after technical explanations

When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation (measurement theory, statistics,
hardware behavior), end it with a short plain-language synopsis, no jargon and no symbols, so
the reader can check their understanding against the technical version.

**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread; the plain form catches
misunderstandings early, when they are cheap.

**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (a notes entry should already lead with
the why). Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no
synopsis.

##### 0.78.0-5 refactor: jj-lib reads

The facade's internals flip: in-process through jj-lib is now
the default read path, and spawning is the carve-out rather
than the mechanism. The seam the DRY-facade cycle bought is
what made this a one-module change: every caller kept its
signature, so push, squash-push, sync, init and the registry
checks moved without being edited.

- The routing is per revset, not per call site, because the
  revs are runtime values: squash-push's source/target default
  to `@`/`@-` but are user-overridable, so no static split of
  the call sites exists. `references_working_copy` decides: a
  `@` is working-copy syntax (`@`, `@-`, `ws@`) unless it has
  symbol characters on both sides, the remote-bookmark form
  (`name@remote`).
- Working-copy revsets keep the spawn path on purpose (the
  ladder's standing caveat): the CLI auto-snapshots, so "is
  `@` empty right now?" answers about the filesystem, while an
  in-process `load_at_head` would answer about the last
  snapshot. Those reads move at `-6` with the mutation lift.

  the facade surface: jj-lib has no template engine (templates
  live in jj-cli), so its one caller, sync's bookmark-heads
  probe, became the typed `cids_short_of`.
- `rev_exists` and sync's `try_commit_id` now classify the
  unresolvable-revision error through one helper,
  `is_no_such_revision`: a typed
  `RevsetResolutionError::NoSuchRevision` downcast on the
  in-process path, the old stderr substrings on the spawn
  path. A first taste of the `-7` principle that

- Parity is pinned by tests: the in-process accessors are
  compared against spawned `jj log` templates on a fixture
  repo, with revs pinned to concrete commit ids so the tests

message.content: I'm confused log is renamed log_spawn and several routines like chid_of use it but have grown more code, explain

content.text:
Before this rung, every helper was a one-liner because there was only one mechanism: build a `jj log -T <template>` argument list and spawn it. `chid_of` was literally just `log(repo, rev, "change_id.short(12)")`.

Now each helper contains **two implementations of the same query**, and picks one at runtime:

```rust
pub fn chid_of(repo: &Path, rev: &str) -> Result<String> {
    if references_working_copy(rev) {
        return log_spawn(repo, rev, "change_id.short(12)");   // path 1: the old code
    }
    Ok(commits_of(repo, rev)?                                  // path 2: new, in-process
        .iter()
        .map(common::format_chid)
        .collect())
}
```

- **Path 1 (spawn)** is the entire old implementation, unchanged, demoted to a private helper. The rename `log` -> `log_spawn` is just labeling: it's no longer "the way reads work", it's "the spawn fallback". It exists because revsets touching the working copy (`@`, `@-`, `@ & empty()`) need jj's auto-snapshot to answer correctly — e.g. push's "does `@` have uncommitted changes *right now*?" — and snapshotting in-process is an op-store write, which this cycle defers to the mutations rung `-6`.
- **Path 2 (in-process)** is where the growth comes from. A spawned `jj` did resolve-revset-and-format for us behind one string template; in-process, those steps become visible Rust: `commits_of` loads the repo and resolves the revset to `Commit` objects, then each helper does in code what its template string used to do — `format_chid` for `change_id.short(12)`, `c.id().hex()` for `commit_id`, `c.description()` for `description`, `commit.is_empty(...)` for `empty`.

So the extra lines aren't added behavior — they're the template language's work being spelled out, plus one `if` deciding which engine answers. At `-6`, when mutations (and snapshotting) move in-process, the `if references_working_copy` branches and `log_spawn` itself are deleted, and each helper shrinks back to just its path-2 body.

Why the branch lives *inside* the helpers rather than at the call sites: the revset is often a runtime value (squash-push's source/target default to `@`/`@-` but the user can override them with anything), so no call site knows statically which engine it needs.

The plain version: the old one-line functions were thin wrappers around one tool, the jj command line. Now each function knows two ways to answer, the new built-in way and the old spawn way, and a small check picks between them. The old code didn't shrink, it moved into `log_spawn`; the new code is the built-in way written out longhand. The check and the spawn path are temporary scaffolding that the mutations rung removes.

content.text:
It's a fair instinct — the scaffolding exists only because reads land before the thing that would make it unnecessary. But I'd keep the order and push -5 as built. The reasoning:

**Why reads-first was chosen (and still holds):**

- **-6 is the risky rung; -5 shrinks it.** The mutation lift is the workspace/transaction/op-store machinery — the part of this cycle that can actually corrupt state and the reason the version gate exists. Landing reads first means -6's diff is *only* the dangerous part, reviewed on its own, with the resolve/format machinery already proven in production for a rung's worth of real use. Merged, one push changes every read *and* every write in the same diff, and a regression found later bisects to "the giant commit".
- **Reverting stays cheap.** If in-process reads turn out to misbehave somewhere, -5 reverts without touching mutations. If -6 misbehaves, it reverts without taking the reads with it. A merged rung couples their fates.
- **The scaffolding is smaller than it looks, and half of it survives -6.** `log_spawn` dies at -6, but the `references_working_copy` classification probably doesn't: even fully in-process, "is `@` empty right now?" still needs a *snapshot first, then read* step that plain reads don't. The likely -6 shape is that the same check routes to "snapshot, then answer" instead of "spawn". So the part of -5 that took actual thought — knowing which revsets are working-copy-relative — is a keeper; only the one-line spawn fallback is throwaway.

**Why -6-first doesn't win:** it would avoid the two-path helpers, but the cost is inverted risk ordering — the op-store lift would land with zero of its read-side machinery pre-validated, and -5 afterwards would be a near-trivial rung. You'd be spending review attention on the safe part after the dangerous part already shipped.

**And practically:** -5 is built, validated, and its cost is already paid. Reordering now means discarding or reshaping done work to avoid scaffolding that -6 deletes in a few days anyway.

If we were standing at cycle open with nothing built, "merge them" would be a defensible call — the counterargument would be diff size and blast radius, and reasonable people could land either way. From where we are, separate-and-in-this-order is better on every axis except "temporary `if` branches exist for one rung".

The plain version: the extra code you noticed is temporary, but it's the cheap kind of temporary — a small detour that lets the scary step (-6) arrive alone, small, and easy to check. Combining the steps would save the detour but make the scary step bigger and harder to undo. I recommend pushing -5 as is and letting -6 delete the detour.
